title: 8-Ball Rules Explained: A Beginner's Guide to Solids, Stripes and the Black 8
description: New to 8-ball? Learn how the break, open table, called pockets, fouls and the black 8 work, plus where house rules differ, in plain English.
body:
Quick: you walk into a bar, someone slides you a cue, and says "8-ball, you break." Do you know what happens next? With the Mosconi Cup warming up the pool world this weekend, plenty of new fans are picking up a cue for the first time. Here is a friendly guide to the most-played pool game on the planet.

The goal of 8-ball

Eight-ball uses all 15 object balls plus the white cue ball. One player gets the solid balls (1 to 7), the other gets the stripes (9 to 15). You must pocket all seven of your balls, then sink the black 8 ball to win. Simple, right? The tricky part is the details.

Racking and breaking

The 15 balls go in a triangle, with the 8 ball in the middle of the third row and a solid and a stripe in the two back corners. Need a refresher? See our guide to racking pool balls. One player breaks, and the break must send balls toward the pockets or the rails. Tips for a stronger opening shot are in how to break in pool.

The table starts "open"

After the break, nobody owns a group yet. This is called an open table. The first player to legally pocket a called ball after the break chooses solids or stripes, and the other player gets the rest. In the official World Pool-Billiard Association (WPA) rules, sinking a ball on the break does not by itself decide groups, so the table normally stays open until a ball is legally made afterwards. Always agree on this before you play, since house rules vary.

Calling your shots

Under standard tournament rules you must call the ball and the pocket for each shot. You do not need to describe bank shots or combinations in detail, but the ball and pocket should be obvious. Many bar and casual games relax this, so a quick "call it or slop?" chat with your opponent saves arguments.

What counts as a foul?

A foul gives your opponent ball in hand, meaning they can place the cue ball anywhere on the table. Common fouls include:

  • Scratching, which means the cue ball goes into a pocket or off the table.
  • Hitting the wrong group first, or the 8 ball first before your group is cleared.
  • Not hitting any ball at all.
  • Making no ball hit a rail after contact, when no ball is pocketed.
  • Knocking an object ball off the table.

We break these down further in pool fouls explained.

Winning (and losing) on the 8 ball

Once all seven of your balls are gone, the 8 ball is your target. Call the pocket, then sink it. Here is where games swing wildly:

  • You win by legally pocketing the 8 in the pocket you called.
  • You lose if you pocket the 8 early, before clearing your group.
  • You lose if you pocket it in a pocket you did not call, or knock it off the table.
  • You lose if you scratch while pocketing the 8 on the same shot.

What if you only scratch while shooting at the 8, without pocketing it? Under WPA rules that is a regular foul, not an automatic loss, and your opponent gets ball in hand. Some other organizations, including leagues like the APA, treat a scratch on the final shot differently. That is a good reason to check which rules your league or venue uses.

Rules that change from place to place

Bar tables and leagues love their own twists. Ask about these before the first break:

  • Slop or no slop: does a ball that goes in by accident count?
  • Break rules: what happens if the 8 drops on the break (re-rack, or win)?
  • Ball in hand: anywhere on the table, or only behind the head string?
  • Scratch on the 8: automatic loss or simple foul?

League players can find the differences in our guide to joining a pool league.

Three beginner strategy tips

1. Look at the whole table before choosing. On an open table, pick the group with fewer clusters and easier shots. 2. Think about the 8 ball early. If it is stuck on a rail or tied up with your balls, plan how to free it. 3. Learn to play safe. When the shot is tough, a good defensive shot can beat a risky one. Our safety play guide is a great start.

Where to watch the pros

Most professional events are nine-ball, but the rules above are how most of us play at home and in leagues. The Mosconi Cup, running November 27 to 30 at Caribe Royale in Orlando, Florida, is nine-ball and a great way to see top players in action. In the US, ESPN says all four days stream live on ESPN+ (afternoons, 1 to 6 p.m. ET), with ESPN2 carrying Sunday's session. Follow along on our Mosconi Cup 2026 hub, find a local event in our tournament finder, or see what is on near you at this weekend's events.

Quick recap

  • Pocket your group (solids 1-7 or stripes 9-15), then the 8 ball.
  • The table is open after the break until someone legally pockets a called ball.
  • Fouls give your opponent ball in hand.
  • Pocket the 8 early, in the wrong pocket, or while scratching, and you lose.
  • Always confirm the local rules first.

Grab a friend, rack them up, and call your shot. Good luck, and may the 8 ball fall your way!
